content: Beclomethasone dipropionate (BDP) and budesonide (BUD) are both widely used inhaled corticosteroids for the management of chronic asthma. These two medications exhibit distinct pharmacokinetic properties when studied in vitro. However, it remains uncertain whether these differences translate into meaningful clinical differences in terms of efficacy or safety for children and adults with chronic asthma. The objective of this analysis was to evaluate clinical outcomes from studies that directly compared inhaled BDP and BUD in the treatment of chronic asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Airways Group Trial Register (1999), reference lists of relevant articles, and abstracts from major respiratory society meetings between 1997 and 1999. Additionally, trialists and pharmaceutical companies were contacted to identify any unpublished studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were prospective, randomized trials that compared BDP and BUD in the treatment of chronic asthma. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the studies and determined their eligibility for inclusion. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer, and missing information was clarified by contacting the study authors. Quantitative analyses were conducted using Review Manager software. A total of 24 studies, involving 1174 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The methodological quality of these studies varied. A meta-analysis of crossover trials did not reveal significant differences between BDP and BUD in terms of forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), morning peak expiratory flow (PEF), evening PEF, asthma symptoms, or the use of rescue beta2-agonists. These findings were based on a dose range of 400 to 1000 mcg/day. However, many of the crossover trials had significant design limitations, such as inadequate washout periods or failure to account for carryover effects, which necessitate cautious interpretation of the results. One crossover study with an adequate washout period suggested that BUD at a dose of 400 mcg/day, delivered via a Turbohaler dry powder inhaler (DPI), might be more effective than BDP at the same dose delivered via a Rotahaler DPI in reducing histamine-induced bronchial hyper-responsiveness. The weighted mean difference (WMD) for log10 PC20 FEV1 was 0.43 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.05 to 0.81). A meta-analysis of two parallel-group, dose down-titration studies involving 231 adult patients indicated that a lower dose of BUD delivered via a Turbohaler DPI was required to maintain asthma control compared to BDP delivered via a metered-dose inhaler (MDI), with or without a spacer. The WMD for the required dose was 444 mcg/day (95% CI: 332 to 556 mcg/day). The authors concluded that there is limited high-quality randomized controlled trial data directly comparing the efficacy of BDP and BUD. Current asthma management guidelines, such as those from the British Thoracic Society (BTS 1997), the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA 1995), and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI 1997), assume that BDP and BUD have equivalent efficacy, recommending the same doses for each medication at defined levels of asthma severity. While some evidence suggests that BUD delivered via a Turbohaler may be more effective than BDP delivered via a Rotahaler or MDI (with or without a spacer), these findings are confounded by differences in the delivery devices used. Consequently, the available evidence is insufficient to justify changes to current guideline recommendations.
